title: Hiking & Outdoor Equipment Stores
one_liner: Specialty outdoor retailers are benefiting from record participation in hiking and outdoor recreation, but 2025-2026 sales are being squeezed by tariffs, higher prices, weaker unit demand and competition from mass, online and athletic retailers.
overview: This industry consists of brick-and-mortar retailers that primarily sell hiking, camping and outdoor sports equipment, apparel and footwear; it excludes online-only sellers, general sporting goods stores and sport-specific shops. Demand is supported by sustained outdoor recreation participation, especially hiking, camping, trail use and casual outdoor fitness, but specialty stores face persistent pressure from Amazon, Walmart, Target, Costco, DICK'S, Academy, Sierra/TJX and brand-direct ecommerce. Public 2025-2026 data point to a mixed market: participation is at record highs, but outdoor retail unit sales weakened as average prices rose, leaving revenue growth more dependent on price, footwear, accessories, repair services and disciplined inventory than on broad volume expansion.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: estimated $7.35 billion in US specialty hiking and outdoor equipment store revenue, derived from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $7.054 billion grown at the baseline projected 2022-2028 CAGR of 1.39%.
key_stats.growth: 2025: estimated +1.4% annual revenue growth for the narrow specialty-store industry; 2026: public OIA channel data show Q1 2026 outdoor ASSG dollars down less than 1% year over year while units fell 7.3%.
key_stats.outdoor_retail_market: 2024: OIA reported $28.0 billion in US outdoor retail sales, up 1.0% from 2023 across broader outdoor retail channels.
key_stats.participation: 2025: OIA reported 183.2 million Americans participated in outdoor recreation, equal to 59% of the US population ages 6 and older.
key_stats.hiking_participation: 2024: OIA reported a record 63.4 million US hikers, equal to 20.5% of Americans ages 6 and older.
key_stats.broader_retail_signal: 2025: BLS/FRED sectoral output for NAICS 4511 sporting goods, hobby and musical instrument stores was $92.758 billion, up 2.1% from $90.889 billion in 2024 but below $94.022 billion in 2022.
key_stats.profitability: 2022: baseline EBIT margin was 3.4%; 2027 baseline forecast was 3.5%, implying structurally thin specialty retail margins.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: +4.7% annual revenue growth after a 10.4% pandemic-driven revenue decline in 2020 and a 9.7% rebound in 2021.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: apparel 30.3% of revenue, equipment and gear 26.4%, footwear 26.4%, other services and products 16.9%.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from sales of outdoor apparel, hiking footwear, camping equipment, backpacks, technical gear, navigation and safety products, accessories, private-label merchandise, classes, events, rentals, repair services and installation services such as racks or bike maintenance. The strongest stores combine product curation with expert advice, fit services, local outdoor community events, loyalty programs, ecommerce fulfillment and used-gear or repair offerings that are harder for pure marketplaces to replicate.

cost_structure.merchandise_purchases: 2025 estimate: largest cost, roughly 50%-60% of revenue, driven by wholesale apparel, footwear, packs, tents and hardgoods costs; tariff exposure increased pressure in 2025-2026.
cost_structure.labor: 2022 baseline: wages were $826 million, equal to about 11.7% of $7.054 billion revenue; 2027 baseline forecast was $860.2 million.
cost_structure.rent_and_store_occupancy: 2025 estimate: meaningful fixed cost for high-traffic retail locations, with pressure partly offset by store rationalization and omnichannel sales.
cost_structure.marketing_and_loyalty: 2025 estimate: rising importance of digital marketing, loyalty rewards, events, classes and local community activation.
cost_structure.freight_and_logistics: 2025-2026: elevated by import, shipping and fulfillment complexity, especially for bulky equipment and ecommerce returns.

current_dynamics: The demand base is expanding, but spending is uneven. OIA's 2026 participation data show outdoor recreation reached 183.2 million US participants in 2025, while hiking reached 63.4 million participants in 2024. At the same time, OIA's retail summaries show 2025 outdoor product sales in athletic specialty and sporting goods channels finished slightly below 2024 levels as tariffs and price increases dampened demand. Q1 2026 continued that pattern: dollar sales were nearly flat, but units fell 7.3% and average retail prices rose 6.7%. Specialty stores are responding with tighter inventories, used gear, repairs, private brands, experiential stores, community programming and omnichannel fulfillment.
whats_growing: 2024-2025: hiking participation and casual outdoor participation continued growing, widening the customer funnel for entry-level footwear, apparel and day-use gear.
2024-2026: footwear, running-inspired outdoor shoes, accessories, backpacks, gear maintenance and repair services are outperforming technical equipment categories.
2025-2026: used gear, repair and resale programs are gaining relevance as price-sensitive consumers delay replacement purchases.
2025-2026: experiential formats, local events, classes and fitting services are becoming more important differentiators for physical stores.
2025-2026: diverse and older participant cohorts are expanding, including strong OIA-reported participation gains among Black, Hispanic, youth and senior consumers.
whats_shrinking: 2025: outdoor equipment unit volumes softened, with OIA reporting overall equipment weakness despite pockets of backpacking, water sports and maintenance growth.
2025-2026: discretionary big-ticket gear replacement is pressured by higher prices, tariffs and weaker middle- and lower-income consumer sentiment.
2022-2027 baseline: underperforming stores and small operators are expected to decline as ecommerce and big-box competition intensify.
2025-2026: full-price technical apparel demand is more selective, with growth concentrated in lifestyle-oriented products rather than purely technical categories.
recent_developments: Apr 2025: OIA warned that new US tariffs would raise costs for outdoor gear companies, with 84% of surveyed OIA members expecting impact.
Apr 2025: OIA reported US outdoor retail sales reached $28.0 billion in 2024, up 1.0% from 2023, with footwear and accessories stronger than equipment and apparel.
May 2026: REI reported 2025 net sales of $3.54 billion, up slightly from 2024, with gross profit up 7% year over year and net loss narrowed to $54.3 million.

Mar 2026: DICK'S reported fiscal 2025 DICK'S Business comparable sales growth of 4.5%, but noted outdoor equipment declines; it ended fiscal 2025 with 35 House of Sport stores and 3 Public Lands stores.
Mar 2026: OIA reported 2025 outdoor ASSG retail sales finished slightly below 2024 levels as tariff-driven price increases reduced unit sales.
Q1 2026: OIA reported outdoor ASSG dollar sales down less than 1%, unit sales down 7.3% and average retail prices up 6.7% year over year.
outlook: Revenue should grow slowly through 2026-2028 if participation remains high, but real volume growth is likely to lag headline sales until prices, tariffs and consumer sentiment stabilize. Specialty winners will be stores with credible expertise, strong loyalty economics, repair/resale programs, footwear strength, local community engagement and integrated ecommerce. Smaller operators without buying scale or a clear niche remain vulnerable to margin compression and customer leakage to Amazon, mass merchants, DICK'S, Academy, Sierra/TJX and brand-direct channels. A reasonable 2026 estimate for the narrow specialty-store industry is about $7.45 billion in revenue, assuming the baseline 1.39% CAGR from 2022, but public channel data suggest downside risk if unit declines persist.
themes: Record outdoor participation, weaker purchase frequency
Competition from mass, ecommerce and broad sporting goods retailers

title: Invoice Factoring
one_liner: Specialty finance firms buy B2B receivables at a discount to give small and midsize companies faster working capital.
overview: The industry provides short-term working capital by purchasing unpaid invoices and collecting from the account debtor, earning factor fees, discount income and ancillary service fees. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline put US invoice factoring revenue at $3.863 billion, with profit of $1.198 billion and a 31.0% margin in 2022. Public 2025-2026 indicators point to stronger activity than the 2022 forecast expected: SFNet reported 2025 factoring volume among long-term respondents rising from $119.4 billion in 2024 to $139.2 billion in 2025, while banks continued to report relatively tight business lending standards and small firms still faced high short-maturity borrowing costs.

key_stats.market_size: $3.0 billion US invoice factoring revenue in 2025, based on publicly indexed IBISWorld citation; SFNet respondent factoring volume was $139.2 billion in 2025.
key_stats.growth: 2025 factoring volume increased 16.6% year over year among SFNet long-term respondents; H1 2025 volume increased 3.5% among comparable respondents.
key_stats.credit_performance: 2025 write-offs were about 0.01% of factoring volume in SFNet survey data.
key_stats.interest_rate_context: Federal funds target range was 3.50%-3.75% on July 29, 2026; NFIB reported 7.4% average interest on short-maturity small-business loans in June 2026.

baseline_2022.growth: Revenue declined 1.6% in 2022 and grew at a 0.1% annualized rate over 2017-2022.
baseline_2022.product_mix: Non-recourse factoring was 69.2% of 2022 revenue, recourse factoring 20.1%, and reverse factoring 10.7%.

how_it_makes_money: Factors advance a percentage of an approved invoice, collect the full invoice from the customer, and keep a discount, factor fee, interest-like yield, reserve spread or service charge. Larger operators also monetize credit checks, collections, payments, fuel-card programs, back-office automation, working-capital facilities and embedded freight-finance tools.

cost_structure.main_costs: Funding costs, credit losses, collections and verification staff, sales commissions, technology, compliance, servicing and bad-debt reserves.
cost_structure.funding_costs: Higher 2025-2026 short-term rates raise warehouse-line and bank-funding expense, pressuring spreads unless fees reprice.
cost_structure.labor: Wages were $455.9 million in 2022; automation is reducing labor intensity in onboarding, invoice verification and collections.
cost_structure.credit_losses: SFNet reported 2025 factoring write-offs near 0.01% of volume, reflecting strong collateral controls, but bankruptcies and disputed invoices remain the key tail risks.
cost_structure.technology: Digital underwriting, API invoice verification, instant payments and fraud controls are increasingly required competitive investments.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Tighter bank credit and lengthening payment terms are increasing demand for factoring, especially among lower-middle-market borrowers that no longer qualify for bank lines or asset-based lending. At the same time, elevated interest rates raise factors' own cost of funds and make price transparency more important. Freight factoring remains the most visible growth battleground, with instant funding, fuel cards, broker credit checks and back-office automation used to retain carriers. Non-recourse factoring dominates volume, but operators are tightening verification and fraud controls as debtor quality and invoice dilution risk become more important.
whats_growing: Non-recourse factoring, which SFNet reported at about 86.8% of 2025 volume.
Freight and logistics factoring platforms offering 24/7 instant funding and broker-payment intelligence.
Factoring demand from borrowers facing tighter bank lending standards and slower customer collections in 2025.
Embedded receivables finance inside accounting, TMS, payments and B2B commerce workflows.
Reverse factoring and broader supply-chain finance for larger buyers and suppliers.
whats_shrinking: Pure recourse factoring share, which was 20.1% of IBIS revenue in 2022 and about 13% of 2025 SFNet volume.
Manual underwriting and paper-heavy invoice verification workflows.
Small standalone factors without low-cost funding, fraud analytics or differentiated industry niches.
Client counts in some transportation niches, as SFNet noted 2025 consolidation even while volume rose.
Demand from borrowers that can still obtain cheaper bank lines or SBA-backed credit.
recent_developments: 2025-02-26: Triumph Financial agreed to acquire Greenscreens.ai to add freight pricing intelligence to its payments, factoring and data platform.
2025-07: Federal Reserve SLOOS reported tighter C&I lending standards and weaker demand for loans to firms of all sizes in Q2 2025.
2025-09-29: SFNet's H1 2025 survey reported factoring volume up 3.5% and funds in use up 13% among comparable respondents.
2025-11-18: OTR Solutions acquired TruckSmarter's approximately $300 million factoring and banking portfolio, expanding its freight-finance footprint.
2026-04-14: SFNet reported 2025 factoring volume up 16.6% year over year, from $119.4 billion in 2024 to $139.2 billion in 2025.
2026-07-29: The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50%-3.75%, keeping short-term funding costs elevated for lenders and borrowers.
outlook: Factoring revenue should be steadier than the 2022 baseline forecast because 2025 demand has strengthened as banks stay selective and payment cycles lengthen. Growth will be uneven: transportation, staffing, manufacturing, construction and government-contracting receivables should remain active, while strong borrowers will still refinance into cheaper bank credit when available. Margin pressure will persist from funding costs, customer price shopping and technology spend, so the winners are likely to be scaled platforms with cheaper capital, automated verification, strong debtor data and cross-sell economics.
themes: Tight bank credit revives nonbank working-capital demand
Freight finance becomes a payments and data platform business
Instant funding and API verification reshape customer expectations
Fraud controls and debtor-risk analytics become core infrastructure
Consolidation favors scaled factors with low-cost capital

title: Meal Kit Delivery Services
one_liner: Meal kits have moved from pandemic-era subscription surge to a broader convenience-food market spanning cook-at-home kits, heat-and-eat meals, grocery pickup and delivery apps.
overview: Meal kit delivery services sell pre-portioned ingredients, recipes and prepared or semi-prepared meals to households through direct-to-consumer subscriptions, one-time online orders, grocery channels and delivery-platform integrations. The category expanded rapidly in 2020 and 2021 as consumers cooked at home, then reset as churn, food inflation, shipping costs and restaurant competition exposed weak unit economics. By 2025 and 2026, the market is larger than the 2022 IBIS baseline, but the operating model has changed: leading brands are pushing higher average order values, prepared meals, fewer unprofitable discounts, in-store availability and partnerships with broader food platforms.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. revenue estimated at $15.2935 billion; 2026 U.S. revenue estimated at $17.4149 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2026-2033 U.S. CAGR forecast at 7.3%; 2026 implied growth from the 2025 estimate is about 13.9%.
key_stats.largest_segment: 2025 cook-and-eat was the largest U.S. offering segment; 2025 cook-and-eat revenue share reported at 69.46%.
key_stats.fastest_growing_segment: 2026-2033 heat-and-eat is identified as the fastest-growing U.S. offering segment.
key_stats.market_context: 2025 U.S. represented 38.8% of global meal kit delivery services revenue in Grand View Research/Horizon Databook estimates.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 IBISWorld U.S. industry revenue: $6.920 billion in 2022 dollars.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue growth: 3.3%; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: 19.0%; 2020 revenue growth: 78.2%; 2021 revenue growth: 30.8%.
baseline_2022.concentration: 2022 four largest companies accounted for an estimated 88.9% of industry revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Operators make money by selling recurring subscriptions, one-time meal kit boxes, premium add-ons, prepared heat-and-eat meals, family plans, diet-specific plans, grocery-shelf meal solutions and private-label or platform-distributed products. Revenue is driven by active customers, order frequency, meals per order, average order value, delivery fees and the ability to convert trial discounts into retained full-price customers.
cost_structure: The largest costs are ingredients, refrigerated fulfillment labor, packaging, ice packs and insulation, last-mile delivery, spoilage, customer acquisition, discounts and technology. The 2022 IBIS baseline showed only a 3.8% profit margin because perishable logistics and promotional churn limited operating leverage; 2025-2026 leaders are responding with fewer low-return promotions, prepared-meal scale, higher basket sizes and asset-light production partnerships.
major_players: HelloFresh SE: HelloFresh, Green Chef, EveryPlate, Factor and Good Chop
Home Chef: Kroger-owned meal solutions brand with subscription, in-store, pickup and delivery distribution
Blue Apron: Wonder-owned brand integrated into Wonder's meal platform after the 2023 acquisition
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is growing in dollar terms, but incumbent meal-kit subscriptions face pressure from churn, grocery meal solutions, restaurant delivery and cautious consumers. HelloFresh reported 2025 group revenue of €6.7608 billion and 2025 North America revenue of €4.2071 billion, down 16.5% from 2024, while its 2026 Q1 update said meal-kit revenue trends improved for the fifth consecutive quarter but were still down 8.5% year over year in constant currency. The industry is therefore bifurcating: market-wide estimates show U.S. growth, while legacy subscription-heavy operators are rationalizing marketing and shifting toward profitable customers, prepared meals and flexible ordering.
whats_growing: Heat-and-eat meals, flexible non-subscription ordering, higher-protein and health-positioned meals, value meal kits, grocery-linked distribution, prepared meals for busy households, and platform bundles that place meal kits alongside restaurant delivery are growing in 2025-2026. HelloFresh's 2026 Q1 release highlighted higher average order value, fewer discounts and more add-ons, while Wonder's 2025 brand refresh positioned Blue Apron meal kits inside a broader mealtime app.
whats_shrinking: Pure weekly subscription dependence, aggressive first-box discounting, low-value customer acquisition, stand-alone public meal-kit models and traditional cook-from-scratch boxes as the only format are shrinking. HelloFresh's 2025 North America revenue decline and 2026 Q1 meal-kit revenue decline show pressure on legacy volume, even as overall U.S. category estimates continue to rise.
recent_developments: 2023-11: Wonder completed its acquisition of Blue Apron, making Blue Apron a wholly owned subsidiary and removing its Class A common stock from Nasdaq.
2023-11: Wonder began offering Blue Apron meal kits and heat-and-eat options through Wonder locations in New York and New Jersey, including non-subscription meal-kit access.
2025-09: Wonder refreshed its brand after the Grubhub and Blue Apron acquisitions and positioned the app as a multi-format mealtime platform including Blue Apron meal kits.
2026-03: HelloFresh reported FY 2025 net revenue of €6.7608 billion and about 850 million meals delivered globally in 2025.

2026-05: HelloFresh reported 2026 Q1 revenue of about €1.7 billion, down 7.7% year over year in constant currency, with meal-kit revenue down 8.5% and ready-to-eat revenue down 6.9% in constant currency.
2026-03: Grand View Research/Horizon Databook updated its U.S. outlook to $15.2935 billion in 2025 revenue, $17.4149 billion in 2026 revenue and a 2026-2033 CAGR of 7.3%.
outlook: The U.S. market should keep expanding through 2026 as consumers keep paying for convenience, portion control and at-home meal variety, but profit will depend less on headline subscriber growth and more on retention quality, basket size, fulfillment density and format mix. Operators with grocery access, prepared-meal capacity, owned logistics or large cross-selling platforms are better positioned than stand-alone subscription brands. The 2026-2033 U.S. CAGR forecast of 7.3% suggests a durable category, but company results point to a more disciplined, lower-discount industry than the 2020-2021 boom.

title: Orthopedic Products Manufacturing
one_liner: US orthopedic product manufacturers make braces, supports, implants and related devices for aging, injury-prone and surgery-dependent patients.
overview: Orthopedic Products Manufacturing covers US production of devices that support, correct or replace bones, joints and muscles, including knee, hip, foot, ankle, neck, back and other orthopedic supports and implants. The 2025 market is larger than the 2022 baseline but still mature: IBISWorld's April 2025 report placed revenue at $12.6 billion in 2025 after a 0.5% CAGR from 2020 to 2025. Demand is anchored by physician offices, outpatient centers, pharmacies, health stores and hospitals, with growth tied to the 64.6 million US residents age 65+ in 2025 and the shift of joint procedures into ambulatory surgical centers. Large diversified medtech companies dominate higher-value implants and robotic surgery ecosystems, while smaller firms compete in braces, orthotics and niche devices.

key_stats.growth: 0.5% revenue CAGR from 2020 to 2025; 1.1% revenue decline in 2023
key_stats.global_context: $64.6 billion projected global orthopedic sales in 2025, up 4.3% from 2024
key_stats.demographic_driver: 64.6 million US residents age 65+ in 2025, up 16.2% from April 1, 2020
key_stats.outpatient_channel: 600+ US ASCs identified as performing total joint replacement procedures in 2025

baseline_2022.growth: 2.7% annualized revenue growth from 2017 to 2022; 0.2% revenue growth in 2022

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell braces, orthotics, supports, surgical implants and related devices to physician offices, outpatient centers, pharmacies, health stores, wholesalers and hospitals. The 2022 baseline split revenue across outpatient care centers and physician offices at 54.4%, health stores and pharmacies at 37.2%, and hospitals at 8.4%. Higher-value revenue comes from implantable knee, hip, trauma, extremity and spine products sold into surgical channels, while lower-cost supports and braces move through retail, pharmacy and clinician dispensing channels.
cost_structure: Major costs include titanium, stainless steel, plastics, silicone, foam, electronics, packaging, outsourced precision machining, sterilization, regulatory compliance, quality systems, R&D, clinical education, sales reps and inventory consignment sets. The 2022 baseline profit margin was 5.6%, signaling limited average pricing power outside the largest branded implant makers. In 2025, tariff exposure and global component sourcing added cost risk for medical-device manufacturers, while hospitals and payers continued to pressure implant pricing and reimbursement.
major_players: Stryker: 2025 Orthopaedics net sales were $9.469 billion, including $2.656 billion knees, $1.865 billion hips and $3.948 billion trauma and extremities.
Zimmer Biomet: 2025 net sales were $8.232 billion, up 7.2% reported and 3.9% organic constant currency.
Johnson & Johnson MedTech / DePuy Synthes: 2025 Orthopaedics sales were $9.258 billion, up 1.1% reported; Johnson & Johnson announced an intended separation of Orthopaedics in 2025.
Smith+Nephew: 2025 Orthopaedics revenue was $2.437 billion, up 5.7% reported and 5.1% underlying.
Orthopediatrics: 2025 revenue was $236.3 million, up 15% from 2024, focused on pediatric trauma, deformity, scoliosis and specialty bracing.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 industry is split between healthy procedure demand and tougher economics. Aging, obesity, sports injuries and outpatient surgery support volume, while hospital procurement teams push down implant prices and device makers absorb higher input, tariff and compliance costs. Robotics, navigation, cementless knees, direct-anterior hip systems and extremities are attracting investment, but mature hip and knee categories are growing more slowly than enabling technology and sports medicine. Consolidation remains active as large manufacturers acquire robotics, software, specialty implants and niche product portfolios.
whats_growing: Robotics and navigation platforms, cementless knees, shoulder and extremity systems, trauma products, sports medicine, outpatient joint replacement, pediatric specialty implants and contract manufacturing are growing. Global orthopedic enabling technology was projected at $1.545 billion in 2025, up 8.7% from 2024, and the US orthopedic contract manufacturing market was valued at $2.8 billion in 2025 with a projected 12.98% CAGR from 2026 to 2033.
whats_shrinking: Lower-differentiation braces and commodity supports face private-label, import and retail pricing pressure. Some legacy spine and sports portfolios are shrinking or being rationalized: Johnson & Johnson's 2025 Spine, Sports & Other Orthopaedics sales fell 2.5%, and Smith+Nephew reported US Knee Implants down 10.3% in Q1 2026. Implant-price pressure also remains structural, with a 2026 Journal of Arthroplasty study finding inflation-adjusted primary TKA implant prices down 38% and primary THA implant prices down 37% from 2009 to 2021.
recent_developments: 2025-02-19: Stryker completed its acquisition of Inari Medical, expanding beyond orthopaedics into peripheral vascular devices.
2025-08-28: Becker's identified 600+ US ASCs performing total joint replacements in 2025, highlighting procedure migration to outpatient settings.
2025-10-07: Zimmer Biomet completed its Monogram Technologies acquisition, adding AI-driven semi-autonomous orthopedic robotics.
2025-10-14: Johnson & Johnson announced plans to separate its Orthopaedics business as standalone DePuy Synthes within an 18-24 month target window.
2026-05-06: Smith+Nephew reported US Knee Implants declined 10.3% in Q1 2026 ahead of its LANDMARK Knee System rollout.
2026-06-24: CMS projected 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth at 5.4% annually, with Medicare spending projected to grow 7.7% annually.
outlook: Revenue should keep expanding modestly through 2026 as aging demographics, Medicare spending and outpatient orthopedic procedures support demand. The best growth is likely in robotics-enabled implants, extremities, trauma, sports medicine and contract manufacturing, while commodity supports and mature knee and hip lines remain price-sensitive. Tariffs, hospital purchasing pressure, FDA compliance costs and global sourcing complexity will limit margin expansion unless manufacturers can offset costs through automation, premium products, pricing, mix improvement or supply-chain redesign.
sources: Local baseline file: /home/manishmehta/ui-projects/ibis-industries/txt_full/orthopedic-products-manufacturing.txt, IBISWorld report last updated 2022-07-01
one_sentence: The industry is growing slowly but steadily in 2025, supported by aging demographics, outpatient orthopedic procedures and robotics-enabled implants, while import competition, hospital price pressure and 2025-2026 tariff uncertainty keep margins tight.

title: Portfolio Management in the US
one_liner: US portfolio managers earn fees on client assets, with market gains lifting AUM while passive products, ETFs and scale economics keep pressure on fee rates.
overview: Portfolio Management in the US comprises firms with discretion to manage client portfolios for fees, including mutual fund managers, ETF sponsors, separate-account managers, hedge fund and private-market managers, pension and insurance mandate managers, and wealth-platform portfolio programs. The baseline IBISWorld file estimated 2022 revenue at $403.3 billion, with 2022 growth of 2.1% and a 2022 profit margin of 36.1%. Applying the baseline 2022-2027 forecast path implies roughly $442.1 billion of 2025 revenue, while current 2025-2026 industry data show a much larger asset base: SEC-registered investment advisers reported $176.8 trillion in 2025 regulatory AUM, up 22.3% from 2024, and US ETF assets reached $13.37 trillion in December 2025 and $15.60 trillion by May 2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated revenue: $442.1 billion, derived from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $403.3 billion and its 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 3.1%.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated revenue growth path: 3.1%; SEC-registered adviser regulatory AUM grew 22.3% in 2025 to $176.8 trillion.
key_stats.aum: 2025 SEC-registered adviser regulatory AUM: $176.8 trillion; 2024 SEC IA statistics reported $146 trillion RAUM, up 12.8% from 2023.
key_stats.etf_assets: US ETF assets were $13.37 trillion in December 2025 and $15.60 trillion in May 2026.
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline profit margin: 36.1%; 2027 baseline forecast profit margin: 32.6%.
key_stats.employment: 2025 SEC-registered investment adviser non-clerical employment: about 1.1 million, up 7.5% from 2024.

how_it_makes_money: Managers primarily charge asset-based advisory and management fees, usually a percentage of AUM, plus performance fees, carried interest, fund administration fees, securities-lending revenue, platform or model-portfolio fees, and advisory program fees. In 2024, 95.5% of SEC-registered advisers offered an asset-based fee, while only 17.4% used asset-based fees alone, indicating broader use of fixed, hourly and performance-linked pricing.
cost_structure: The largest expense is compensation for portfolio managers, analysts, distribution teams, compliance staff and technology personnel; 2022 baseline wages equaled about 33.2% of revenue. Other major costs include data and research, trading and custody connectivity, fund administration, compliance, cybersecurity, cloud and portfolio systems, marketing and distribution, rent, insurance, and acquired-intangible amortization. Scale matters because index and ETF products require large asset bases to offset very low fees.
major_players: BlackRock: $14.0 trillion AUM at December 31, 2025 after $698 billion of 2025 net inflows.
Vanguard: major low-cost index and ETF provider with more than 50 million investors at December 31, 2025 and a 2025 asset-weighted average US fund and ETF expense ratio of 0.07%.
Fidelity Investments: 2025 managed assets of $7.1 trillion and assets under administration of $18.0 trillion.
State Street Investment Management: $5.62 trillion AUM at March 31, 2026, including SPDR ETF assets.
T. Rowe Price: $1.8 trillion AUM at December 31, 2025.
current_dynamics: Equity-market appreciation, retirement savings, ETF adoption and adviser-channel growth are expanding AUM, but fee yields continue to compress as investors shift toward low-cost passive products and institutional buyers demand scale pricing. Traditional active mutual funds face outflows and margin pressure, while ETFs, fixed income, model portfolios, private markets, separately managed accounts and outsourced CIO mandates are gaining share. Compliance obligations and technology investment remain heavy, and consolidation continues as large platforms acquire distribution, data, private-market capabilities and adviser relationships.
whats_growing: ETFs, index strategies, fixed-income funds, cash and money-market products, retirement assets, model portfolios, separately managed accounts, private credit, infrastructure, wealth-management platforms, outsourced CIO mandates, and AI-enabled operations and portfolio analytics are growing. ICI reported record 2025 ETF net issuance of $1.5 trillion and ETF assets above $13 trillion at year-end 2025.
whats_shrinking: High-fee active equity mutual funds, traditional closed-end funds, standalone subscale active managers, and simple asset-based pricing without planning or advice are losing share. Fee rates are shrinking even when AUM rises, and active equity strategies remain vulnerable to benchmark underperformance and flows into cheaper ETFs.
recent_developments: 2025-04: ICI reported 2024 ETF net issuance reached a record $1.1 trillion and US household fund ownership reached 74 million households.
2025-06: SEC staff noted registered funds held more than $39 trillion and registered investment advisers had about $145.8 trillion RAUM based on 2024 data.
2025-08: SEC updated Investment Adviser Statistics showing 2024 RAUM of $146 trillion, up 12.8% from 2023.
2026-01: BlackRock reported $14.0 trillion AUM at December 31, 2025 after record 2025 net inflows of $698 billion.
2026-04: ICI’s 2026 Fact Book reported 2025 ETF net issuance of $1.5 trillion and worldwide regulated fund assets of $88.0 trillion.
2026-06: IAA and Comply reported 2025 SEC-registered adviser AUM of $176.8 trillion, up 22.3%, with 16,544 advisers.
outlook: Revenue should keep expanding through 2026 as market levels, retirement savings and adviser demand support AUM, but growth will be uneven. Scaled managers with ETF franchises, distribution partnerships, private-market products, advice platforms and operating leverage should outperform, while subscale active managers face persistent outflows, higher technology and compliance spending, and lower realized fee rates. The baseline forecast points to 2027 revenue of $470.9 billion and a lower 2027 profit margin of 32.6%, consistent with fee compression despite AUM growth.
one_sentence: The industry remains large and profitable in 2025-2026, but growth is increasingly captured by low-cost index, ETF, model-portfolio, private-market and wealth-platform providers rather than traditional active mutual fund managers.
